strengths: Compelling results at extreme sparsity regimes: The paper convincingly demonstrates that ELSA maintains reasonable perplexities and downstream zero-shot performance at 80% and 90% sparsity (e.g., perplexity of 23.14 on C4 for LLaMA-2-7B at 90%), where conventional one-shot and layer-wise pruning techniques severely degrade or collapse.

Well-reasoned critique of the status quo: The conceptual discussion in Section 2 regarding the fundamental limitations of layer-wise reconstruction error minimization (REM)—compounding errors, layer independence, and surrogate objective mismatch—provides a clear justification for moving to global end-to-end optimization.

Principled and practical algorithmic design: Combining global ADMM with an objective-aware projection using the diagonal empirical Fisher matrix (retrieved practically for free from Adam's second-moment accumulator) is an elegant design choice. The addition of low-precision state management (ELSA-L) makes the approach scalable to 27B models on modest hardware.

Theoretical grounding: The authors provide convergence analysis for both the standard formulation (ELSA) and the quantized-state variant (ELSA-L), proving convergence to a stationary point under standard non-convex/weakly-convex assumptions.

Extensive experimental breadth: The empirical study evaluates multiple model families (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3/3.2) across parameter scales from 125M to 27B, including unstructured, semi-structured (N:M), and non-uniform sparsity allocations.
weaknesses: Unfair compute/sample budget comparison with baselines: The comparison primarily benchmarks against one-shot post-training pruning methods (SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS, SAFE, L-ADMM), which operate on only 128 calibration sequences without full-model backpropagation. In contrast, ELSA performs full end-to-end iterative training for 4,096 steps with batch size 8 (32,768 sequences) using backward passes across the whole network. This effectively transitions the task from lightweight post-training pruning to full-model sparse fine-tuning, yet comparisons against actual sparse fine-tuning / retraining baselines (e.g., iterative magnitude pruning with fine-tuning or LoRA-based sparse training) are absent.

Lack of wall-clock time and computational overhead analysis: The paper does not report running time, GPU memory consumption (in GB), or total FLOPs required for ELSA compared to one-shot layerwise baselines. Given the full backpropagation requirement across 4k steps, quantifying the exact training cost is critical for practitioners.

Suboptimal performance in low-to-moderate sparsity regimes: At 50% and 60% sparsity, ELSA is consistently outperformed in both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy by existing layer-wise methods such as ALPS, SAFE, and L-ADMM (e.g., Table 6 and Table 7). The authors do not adequately explain why a global end-to-end objective underperforms surrogate layer-wise methods at moderate sparsities.

Unfinished text and typographical errors: Several sentences in the manuscript end abruptly without finishing (e.g., end of Section 5: 'The source code to reproduce results will be made available at'; Appendix B.1: 'training scripts) will be made available at'). There are also typos in the text and algorithm descriptions (e.g., Algorithm 1 line 3 updates 'y' instead of 'z'; Algorithm 1 line 4 has '=0' inside the norm; 'constrat' on page 9).

strengths: Principled and clear motivation: The paper convincingly identifies the fundamental limitations of sequential layer-wise reconstruction error minimization (compounding errors, restricted search space, and objective mismatch) and proposes a mathematically grounded surrogate-free formulation directly optimizing the full language modeling objective.

Comprehensive theoretical backing: The authors formulate pruning as constrained optimization solved via ADMM and provide convergence proofs (to stationary points) for both exact ELSA and the quantized/inexact variant ELSA-L.

Remarkable empirical results at extreme sparsity: In the high-sparsity regime (70%–90%), ELSA significantly outperforms prior pruning baselines, avoiding catastrophic perplexity explosion and preserving substantially higher downstream zero-shot accuracy across multiple architectures (OPT, LLaMA-2/3, Gemma-2).

Scalability considerations: The introduction of ELSA-L (leveraging 8-bit optimizer states and low-precision FP8/BF16 auxiliary ADMM states) demonstrates practical scalability to models up to 27B parameters with reduced GPU memory footprint.
weaknesses: Discrepancy in compute and data budget: While baseline methods like SparseGPT, Wanda, and ALPS operate in a one-shot or layer-wise manner using only 128 calibration sequences with minimal compute overhead (typically minutes on a single GPU), ELSA performs full end-to-end backpropagation across the entire network for 4,096 steps with batch size 8 (~32,768 sequences / ~67M tokens) on multi-GPU setups. Comparing these methods directly without discussing the substantial difference in compute and calibration tokens is somewhat apples-to-oranges.

Sub-optimal performance at moderate sparsity: At standard/moderate sparsity levels (50%), ELSA frequently underperforms existing layer-wise methods. For example, on LLaMA-2-7B at 50% sparsity (Table 6 & Table 7), ELSA achieves lower zero-shot accuracy (53.35% vs. 57.73% for L-ADMM) and higher perplexity, suggesting that global optimization may require further tuning or regularization when the pruning budget is less constrained.

Sensitivity and heterogeneity in hyperparameters: As shown in Table 5, the penalty parameter lambda, learning rate eta, and penalty schedules (constant vs. cosine) require substantial per-model and per-sparsity customization, which may complicate the out-of-the-box adoption of the method for new architectures.

Absence of real-world speedup benchmarks: While unstructured extreme sparsity (90%) yields impressive perplexity preservation, the paper does not report actual wall-clock inference speedups or memory throughput on specialized sparse hardware/kernels, leaving practical latency gains unverified.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant challenge in LLM compression: preventing catastrophic performance degradation at extreme sparsity levels (70%–90%).
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3) and model scales ranging from 125M up to 27B parameters.

The proposal of ELSA-L incorporates low-precision (FP8/INT8) auxiliary state representation to reduce memory overhead during optimization, demonstrating practical engineering effort to scale the method to larger architectures.
Exploration of varied sparsity structures, including unstructured, N:M semi-structured, and non-uniform layer-wise sparsity profiles.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison and compute disparity: ELSA is evaluated against one-shot post-training pruning (PTP) methods (e.g., Wanda, SparseGPT, ALPS, SAFE, L-ADMM) that operate layer-by-layer without end-to-end backpropagation using only 128 calibration sequences. In contrast, ELSA performs 4,096 iterative end-to-end training steps with batch size 8 and sequence length 2048 (~67 million tokens) across multiple A100/H200 GPUs. The paper does not compare against post-training pruning followed by fine-tuning on the same data/compute budget, nor against standard iterative pruning with fine-tuning.

Underperformance at standard sparsity regimes: At 50% and 60% sparsity levels (Tables 1, 6, 7, and 8), ELSA consistently underperforms or at best matches the one-shot layer-wise baselines (e.g., ALPS, SAFE, L-ADMM), despite expending orders of magnitude more compute and backpropagation.

Significant gap between theoretical formulation and practical implementation: Algorithm 1 and Theorem 4.6 assume that the primal subproblem for $x^{t+1}$ is solved to high accuracy ($\|x^{t+1} - x^{t+1}_*\| \le \gamma \dots$) at each outer iteration. In practice, the implementation simply performs a single Adam gradient step per iteration. Consequently, the convergence guarantees do not apply to the actual algorithm executed in the experiments.

Notational errors and inconsistencies in the theoretical presentation: Algorithm 1 contains evident errors (e.g., the loop iterates over index $r$ while expressions use $t$; line 3 updates a variable $y$ that is never referenced again, while lines 4–5 use an undefined $z^{t+1}$). Additionally, in Appendix A (equations 28–29), setting $u^{t+1} = -
abla f(x^{t+1})$ implies $u^{t+1} - u^t = -(
abla f(x^{t+1}) - 
abla f(x^t))$, but the sign is neglected in the subsequent inner product expansion.

Missing global baselines and incomplete evaluation: SparseLLM—the main representative of global optimization—is omitted from Gemma-2-2B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, and LLaMA-2-13B. Furthermore, the paper lacks explicit wall-clock training time comparisons to quantify the computational trade-offs.

strengths: Compelling conceptual shift: The paper convincingly identifies the fundamental limitations of sequential layer-wise reconstruction error minimization (compounding errors, restricted search space, and surrogate overfitting) that cause existing methods to collapse beyond 50-70% sparsity.

Remarkable empirical results at extreme sparsity: ELSA maintains surprisingly strong language modeling capabilities up to 80-90% (and even 95%) sparsity across multiple model architectures (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2/3) and scales (125M to 27B), whereas existing methods suffer catastrophic perplexity blow-ups.

Principled and practical algorithm design: Using ADMM to decouple sparsity constraints while employing an objective-aware projection via the empirical diagonal Fisher information (recycled virtually for free from Adam's second-moment buffers) is elegant and effective.

System and hardware efficiency: The introduction of ELSA-L (using low-precision FP8/INT8 optimizer and auxiliary states) significantly lowers memory overhead, enabling 27B-scale pruning under practical compute constraints. Moreover, inference speedup benchmarks using the MACKO SpMV kernel show tangible real-world speedups (up to 3.98x throughput) on consumer hardware.

Thorough evaluation: The paper includes extensive evaluations on perplexity, 7 zero-shot downstream tasks, matched-compute retraining baselines, non-uniform and semi-structured N:M sparsity, and solid convergence analysis for the quantized ADMM formulation.
weaknesses: Compute and paradigm trade-offs: Unlike truly 'post-training' single-pass pruning methods (such as SparseGPT or Wanda, which execute in minutes on 128 samples), ELSA optimizes over 32k sequences of length 2048 (~4,000 steps). While the authors include Wanda + LoRA / Full retraining baselines to demonstrate that ELSA uses compute much more effectively, ELSA operates more as a sparsity-constrained continual training/fine-tuning framework than a lightweight calibration-based pruner.

Algorithmic novelty: ADMM with $L_0$ projection for neural network weight pruning has an extensive history in deep learning (e.g., Zhang et al., ECCV 2018). While adapting it globally to LLMs with diagonal Fisher projection and low-precision state management is practically impactful, the core optimization framework is well-established.
Missing code repository link: The reproduction URL in Section 5 is left incomplete ('The source code to reproduce results will be made available at ').

strengths: Presents a major breakthrough in LLM pruning by pushing the effective unstructured sparsity frontier up to 80–90% (and exploring up to 99%), where existing layer-wise heuristic methods catastrophically degrade.

Provides a clear and convincing conceptual critique of the standard layer-wise reconstruction surrogate objective, demonstrating why global, surrogate-free optimization directly on next-token prediction is superior at high sparsity.

Introduces well-grounded algorithmic innovations, including objective-aware projection leveraging Adam's second moments (empirical Fisher information) with negligible overhead, and low-precision state management (ELSA-L) to dramatically reduce memory footprint.
Includes theoretical convergence guarantees for both exact ELSA and the quantized-state variant ELSA-L to a stationary point under standard non-convex / weakly convex assumptions.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse model architectures (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2/3) and scales (125M to 27B), covering perplexity, zero-shot downstream benchmarks, and real hardware deployment latency/throughput with the MACKO SpMV kernel.
weaknesses: ELSA operates more as an iterative sparse fine-tuning method (requiring 32k sequences and several GPU-hours) than a classic post-training one-shot pruner (like Wanda or SparseGPT, which run in minutes on 128 samples). While Table 3 shows ELSA outperforms matched-budget Wanda+Full fine-tuning, the framing should more explicitly distinguish the iterative pruning paradigm from one-shot post-training pruning.

Hardware benefits of unstructured sparsity remain constrained on modern Tensor Cores compared to structured (N:M) sparsity. In the 2:4 semi-structured regime (Table 8), ELSA achieves comparable but not superior results to existing layer-wise baselines, indicating that ELSA's primary advantage lies specifically in high unstructured sparsity.
Minor algorithmic/notational inconsistencies, such as in Algorithm 1 (line 3 mentions updating auxiliary variable 'y' rather than 'z').

strengths: Compelling Performance at Extreme Sparsity: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can achieve functional perplexity and retain reasonable downstream accuracy at extreme unstructured sparsity levels (80–90%), where conventional post-training methods catastrophically degrade.

Real Hardware Acceleration and Memory Benchmarks: Rather than relying solely on theoretical FLOPs, the authors benchmark real end-to-end token generation throughput and latency using the MACKO SpMV kernel on an NVIDIA RTX 3090, confirming practical latency reductions (up to 4.0x) and memory savings (up to 7.8x) at 95% sparsity.

Scalability via Low-Precision Auxiliary States (ELSA-L): The proposed ELSA-L variant uses FP8/BF16 representation for ADMM states alongside 8-bit Adam optimizer states, effectively reducing auxiliary memory footprint by 55% and enabling scaling to Gemma-2-27B.

Extensive Model Coverage: The empirical evaluation spans multiple model families (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3.2) across parameter scales from 125M to 27B, including unstructured, semi-structured (N:M), and non-uniform sparsity settings.
weaknesses: Severe Compute and Data Disparity in Primary Comparisons: The narrative attributes the failure of prior works primarily to their sequential layer-wise surrogate formulation. However, baselines such as Wanda, SparseGPT, and ALPS in Figures 1–4 and Table 10 were run in their standard post-training setup with only 128 calibration sequences (~0.26M tokens) and zero or layer-local backpropagation. In contrast, ELSA performs full end-to-end backpropagation over 32,768 sequences (~67M tokens) for thousands of gradient steps. Presenting ELSA against 128-sample post-training pruners as the main baseline comparison creates a misleading impression of the algorithmic advantage.

Omission of Retrained Baselines in Main Benchmarks: Retrained baselines with matched compute (e.g., Wanda + Full fine-tuning, Wanda + LoRA) are only evaluated in Tables 2 and 3 for LLaMA-2-7B. Table 3 shows that Wanda + Full fine-tuning achieves a perplexity of 34.87 (dramatically improving upon one-shot Wanda's >10,000), proving that much of the gap stems from backpropagation compute and data volume. Matched-compute retrained baselines are entirely absent from the broader benchmark results across other architectures, scales, and downstream zero-shot tasks (Figures 2, 4 and Table 10).

Limited Algorithmic Novelty: Formulating neural network pruning as a constrained optimization problem solved via ADMM (variable splitting with an auxiliary variable and projection onto the L0 ball) is a well-established technique in deep learning literature. Furthermore, approximating the diagonal Fisher information matrix via Adam's second-moment accumulator for the projection step directly follows prior work (Li et al., 2025). The algorithmic novelty is therefore modest.

Theoretical Disconnect with the Empirical Algorithm: The convergence analysis in Section 4 and Appendix A (Theorem 4.6) assumes deterministic full-batch gradients and bounded subproblem optimality. In practice, ELSA employs stochastic mini-batch Adam with an update interval of k=32 on a stream of tokens. The deterministic convergence analysis does not cover this stochastic, mini-batch setting, leaving a noticeable gap between the theory and the actual implementation.

 Experiments are conducted on...'), missing the intended repository or citation link.
